newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN panel tells China to respect Hong Kong rights.
newsitem.headline: UN panel tells China to respect Hong Kong rights.

text.p: A U.N. panel told Beijing on Wednesday it should respect human rights in Hong Kong after Britain returns the territory to China in 1997.

The U.N. Human Rights Committee, meeting in Geneva, also said in a statement that China should continue to file regular reports on the situation after the transfer at midnight on June 30, which will end a century and a half of colonial rule.
After that, Hong Kong becomes a Special Administrative Region of China which has promised to keep the area's capitalist lifestyle and a high degree of autonomy until 2047.
The committee of 18 independent experts oversees compliance with the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, a major international human rights treaty.
Britain has signed the 1976 pact but China has not, raising concerns about human rights in Hong Kong in the future.
Even if China was not a party to the treaty, it had "an obligation" to implement it, the committee ruled, according to an official account of the hearing issued by the U.N.

It said they urged China to leave intact Hong Kong's legislative council, elected last year and which China has vowed to dissolve as soon as it takes over, and asked if China would allow political non-governmental groups to operate in Hong Kong.
Henry Steel, an official of the British foreign office, told the meeting his government was continuing to press China to respect the reporting obligations, the statement said.
Hong Kong Solicitor-General Daniel Fung said "respect for human rights in times of emergency was ensured", it added.
Fung leads the Hong Kong group as part of the official British team for the two-day committee hearing which ended on Wednesday.
Beijing has argued that it will have no obligation to the committee after the transfer as it is not a signatory to the Covenant, which the U.N. body monitors.

In a recent interview, Chinese Foreign Minister Qian Qichen suggested public protests over official policies would be barred and Hong Kong's freewheeling media would face restrictions on what it could write after the transfer.
But Fung on Tuesday said other Chinese officials had later said Qian had been misunderstood. The Hong Kong government was seeking clarification from Beijing on the remarks, he added.
